conflicts.situation: Water is on the basement floor (moisture_basement == true), R1 has turned the sump pump on, and home power goes above 6000 W.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R3 switches off the basement circuit. This cuts power to the sump pump while there is still water, so the basement can flood. The chest freezer also loses power.
conflicts.explanation: The sump pump is plugged into a socket on the basement circuit. Switching relay_basement off powers the pump down even though R1 has it switched on, and neither rule checks for this.

conflicts.situation: At 02:00 R4 turns the washer plug on. Its 2.5 kW heating element, on top of the other loads, pushes home_power above 6000 W.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The washer starting causes R3 to cut the basement circuit. The chest freezer shuts down, which can spoil food if nobody notices overnight, and the sump pump loses power.
conflicts.explanation: R4's action raises home_power, which is R3's trigger. R3 then sheds the basement circuit rather than the washer that caused the spike.

conflicts.situation: After 23:30, when R1 has turned off the TV and AV receiver, someone opens the balcony door.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R2 powers the AV receiver back on, and through HDMI-CEC the TV also wakes up, so the TV runs late at night against R1's shutdown.
conflicts.explanation: R2 only targets the receiver, but receiver power-on wakes the TV through CEC. This silently cancels R1's TV-off action.

conflicts.situation: At 19:00, R3 turns on the floor lamp, which shines directly on the bookshelf multisensor.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The light reading goes above 200 lux, so R7 turns the lamp off right after the schedule turned it on, and the room is left without the intended evening light.
conflicts.explanation: The lamp's own light raises lux_living past R7's threshold, so R7 fires because of R3's action.

conflicts.situation: Motion in the living room while it is darker than 30 lux.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R6 turns the lamp on, the sensor reads over 200 lux, and R7 turns it off. The room goes dark, the next motion turns it on again, and the lamp keeps flickering.
conflicts.explanation: The lamp lights the sensor that both rules read, so R6's action triggers R7, and R7's action restores R6's dark condition.

conflicts.situation: At 06:30 R1 turns on the steam shower generator. Steam drifts out through the bathroom door onto the landing, where the photoelectric detector reads it as smoke (smoke_landing = true).
conflicts.undesired_outcome: A false fire alarm: R2 sounds the indoor siren early in the morning and shuts off the air handler that serves the whole home, even though there is no fire.
conflicts.explanation: The steam from R1's action sets off the smoke trigger that R2 listens for. R2 can't tell steam from real smoke, so a normal morning steam shower causes a false alarm and turns off the HVAC.

conflicts.situation: Between 22:00 and 08:00 the pump is off (R1) and the pool temperature drops below 26 C, so R2 fires.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The heater is commanded on but the flow switch keeps or forces the burner off, so the pool isn't heated overnight and the system state is inconsistent.
conflicts.explanation: R1 turns the circulation pump off. The gas heater's flow switch stops the burner when no water circulates, which cancels R2's heating command.

conflicts.situation: The home is in away mode (R7 has turned the heater off) and the pool temperature falls below 26 C.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R2 turns the gas heater back on while nobody is home, which wastes energy and overrides the away-mode shutdown.
conflicts.explanation: R7 sets pool_heater.heating to off and R2 sets it to on. R2 has no away-mode condition, so both rules can fire and give opposite commands to the same device.

conflicts.situation: Occupants leave between 22:00 and 02:00: everyone_away becomes true and living-room motion stops at the same time.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: Hub mode is set to both away (R1) and night (R2); the empty home can end up in night mode, so the away settings (16 C setpoint, camera recording) are overridden.
conflicts.explanation: R1 and R2 write different values to hub.mode and their triggers fire together when the last person leaves late in the evening. The outcome depends on which rule runs last.

conflicts.situation: Late-evening departure (22:00-02:00): the mode goes to away, then R2 switches it to night.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The living-room camera stops recording while the home is empty, defeating the security purpose of R6.
conflicts.explanation: R6 turns camera recording on in away mode and R7 turns it off in night mode. The away-to-night switch caused by R1 and R2 makes both fire in sequence, so the camera ends up off.

conflicts.situation: Every morning: R2 turns the bedroom radiator on at 06:45, then R1 opens the bedroom window at 07:00.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The TRV's window-open detection shuts the radiator valve, so the planned morning heating stops after only 15 minutes and the bedroom stays cold.
conflicts.explanation: Opening the window makes the TRV sense a temperature drop and switch heating off. This undoes R2's heating-on action through a dependency that neither rule mentions.

conflicts.situation: Bedroom CO2 goes above 1000 ppm while the radiator is heating, for example during the morning warm-up R2 starts at 06:45.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R4 opens the window, the TRV detects it and stops heating, so R2's heating goal is defeated.
conflicts.explanation: R4's window-open action reaches trv_bed.heating through the TRV's window-open detection and sets it off, against R2's heating := on.

conflicts.situation: Bedroom CO2 is above 1000 ppm while outdoor PM2.5 is above 35.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R4 opens the window and R5 closes it. The window can flip back and forth, and either polluted air comes in or CO2 stays high.
conflicts.explanation: Both rules can be active at the same time and give opposite commands to window_bed.position (open vs closed).

conflicts.situation: At 07:00, while outdoor PM2.5 is already above 35, so R5 has already closed the window and turned on the purifier.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R1 opens the window anyway. Polluted outdoor air comes in while the purifier runs, which undoes R5's protection.
conflicts.explanation: R1's time-based open command overrides R5's earlier close command on the same window because R1 does not check air quality.

conflicts.situation: At 07:30 while bedroom CO2 is still above 1000 ppm, or CO2 goes above 1000 ppm again soon after R3 closes the window.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R3 closes the window and R4 opens it again, so the window cycles and the 07:30 close schedule is not kept.
conflicts.explanation: R3 sets the window to closed at a fixed time while R4 asks for open under the CO2 condition. Both can apply to the same window at the same moment.

conflicts.situation: Driveway motion turns the floodlight on (R1); the hot halogen housing sits right above the motion sensor.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The sensor keeps reporting motion, so R2 never fires and the floodlight stays on indefinitely, wasting energy.
conflicts.explanation: R1's action (floodlight on) heats the sensor and keeps motion_drive true. That blocks the motion_drive == false trigger R2 needs.

conflicts.situation: Home in night or away mode; the floodlight is on after driveway motion.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: Heat from the floodlight keeps triggering the motion sensor, so the camera records continuously or keeps restarting. This wastes storage and hides real events among false alarms.
conflicts.explanation: R1 turns the floodlight on, its heat sets motion_drive true, and that repeatedly fires R3's recording trigger without a real intruder.

conflicts.situation: After 23:00, when R5 has switched off the outdoor lighting circuit, and motion is detected on the driveway.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R1 switches the floodlight on, but it has no power. The driveway stays dark at night, defeating the security light, and the camera records in the dark.
conflicts.explanation: The floodlight is wired to the outdoor circuit, so R5's relay off overrides R1's floodlight on without either rule mentioning the other.

conflicts.situation: R5 switches the outdoor circuit off at 23:00 and no rule ever turns it back on; at 19:00 the next day R4 turns the garden lights on.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The garden lights stay dark every evening after the first night even though R4 sets them on.
conflicts.explanation: The garden lights get their power from the outdoor relay, which stays off permanently after R5 runs, so R4's action has no effect.

conflicts.situation: A storm with rain and wind above 40 km/h, so raining == true and wind_speed > 40 at the same time
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R3 extends the awning while R2 retracts it. The awning may end up extended in strong wind, which goes against the manufacturer's limit and risks damage, or it keeps switching between positions.
conflicts.explanation: Rain and strong wind often happen together. R3 and R2 then set opposite positions on awning.position, and neither rule checks the other's sensor.

conflicts.situation: A bright, windy day with lux_balcony > 50000 and wind_speed > 40
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R1 extends the awning while R2 retracts it. If R1 fires after R2, for example when a bright spell starts during a gust, the awning is extended in wind above the 40 km/h limit and can be damaged.
conflicts.explanation: R1 extends the awning based only on brightness and does not check wind speed, so it can override the safety retraction from R2.

conflicts.situation: Water is detected on the basement floor (R1 turns sump pump on) while whole-home power exceeds 6000 W (R3 switches relay_basement off).
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The sump pump loses power during a water event, so the basement can flood; R1's intended effect is silently defeated.
conflicts.explanation: The sump pump is plugged into a socket on the basement circuit, so R3's load-shedding relay-off physically cuts the pump's power regardless of R1.

conflicts.situation: At 02:00 R4 turns on the washing machine; its 2.5 kW heating element pushes home_power above 6000 W.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R3 is triggered and shuts off the basement circuit, cutting power to the chest freezer (food may thaw) and the sump pump (no flood protection) until the circuit is restored.
conflicts.explanation: R4's action raises home_power, which is R3's trigger; R3 then de-energises the basement circuit and all devices on it.

conflicts.situation: After 23:30, when R1 has turned the AV receiver off, the balcony door is opened and R2 turns the receiver back on.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The AV receiver turns back on and music plays on the balcony speakers late at night, undoing R1's nightly shutdown.
conflicts.explanation: R1 and R2 set av_receiver.power to opposite states. R2 has no time restriction, so it can override R1 after 23:30.

conflicts.situation: After R1 has turned off the TV and receiver at 23:30, the balcony door opens and R2 powers the receiver on.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The TV wakes up at night even though R1 turned it off.
conflicts.explanation: The TV and receiver are linked by HDMI-CEC, so powering on the receiver also turns on the TV. This dependency isn't stated in either rule.

conflicts.situation: There is motion in the living room and the light reading is below 30 lux, so R6 turns the floor lamp on.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The lamp switches on and off repeatedly, and the room never stays lit.
conflicts.explanation: The lamp shines directly on the multisensor's light sensor, so the reading jumps above 200 lux and R7 turns the lamp off. When it gets dark again, the next motion turns the lamp back on.

conflicts.situation: At 19:00 R3 turns the floor lamp on.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The scheduled evening light is switched off almost immediately.
conflicts.explanation: The lamp's light falls on the multisensor, which pushes lux_living above 200, and R7 turns the lamp off.

conflicts.situation: At 06:30 the steam shower generator turns on; steam drifts from the bathroom onto the landing.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: False smoke alarm: siren sounds and the house-wide air handler is shut off every morning.
conflicts.explanation: R1's steam is read by the photoelectric landing detector as smoke (smoke_landing = true), which triggers R2 unexpectedly.

conflicts.situation: During the 06:30-07:00 steam session, bathroom humidity rises above 75 %.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: Extractor fan turns on and removes the steam the shower is producing, defeating the steam session and wasting energy.
conflicts.explanation: R1 increases humidity_bath, which triggers R5; R5's fan then decreases humidity, counteracting R1's intended effect.

conflicts.situation: From 22:00 until 08:00 the pool pump is off (R1), and the pool water drops below 26 C, so R2 turns the heater on.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The heater's flow switch stops the burner because no water is moving. R2's heating command has no effect, so the pool cools overnight and the heater may keep receiving on commands that fail.
conflicts.explanation: R1 turns off the circulation pump. The gas heater depends on water flow through its built-in flow switch, and R2 does not account for this, so R2 cannot heat the pool while the pump is off.

conflicts.situation: The home is in away mode, so R7 has turned the heater off, and then the pool water drops below 26 C.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R2 turns the gas heater back on while nobody is home. This cancels the away-mode shutdown and burns gas with no one present.
conflicts.explanation: R7 and R2 send opposite commands to pool_heater.heating (off and on). R2 has no condition on home mode, so both rules can fire in the same away period.

conflicts.situation: Everyone leaves the flat between 22:00 and 02:00. R1 sets hub.mode to away, and because the living room is now empty, motion_living becomes false and R2 sets hub.mode to night.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The hub ends up in night mode instead of away while nobody is home. Away-mode behaviour (16 C setpoint, camera recording) is replaced by night-mode behaviour (19 C setpoint, camera off).
conflicts.explanation: R1 and R2 write different values to the same state, hub.mode. Their triggers can fire together because people leaving is exactly what makes living-room motion stop, and R2 does not check presence.

conflicts.situation: Late evening (22:00-02:00): the last person leaves, R1 switches to away and R6 starts recording. Motion then stops in the empty living room, so R2 switches to night and R7 fires.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The living room camera stops recording while the home is empty, which defeats the security purpose of away mode. Heating also goes back up to 19 C (R4), wasting energy.
conflicts.explanation: Leaving the home changes the motion context, which unexpectedly triggers R2's night mode. R7 then turns the camera off, undoing R6's away-mode recording.

conflicts.situation: The household is away (mode away from R1) and motion is detected in the living room between 06:00 and 10:00, for example from a pet, an intruder or a cleaner.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The mode switches to home while nobody is there. Away-mode protections no longer apply (camera recording is no longer tied to the mode) and the away heating setback is lost.
conflicts.explanation: R5 sets hub.mode to home based on motion alone, without checking everyone_away. This overrides the away mode that R1 set.

conflicts.situation: Every morning: R2 turns on heating at 06:45, R1 opens the window at 07:00.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The radiator thermostat's window-open detection shuts the valve, so morning heating stops after 15 minutes and the bedroom is not heated.
conflicts.explanation: The open window makes the radiator thermostat switch heating off, which undoes R2's heating-on action. Neither rule mentions this link.

conflicts.situation: Bedroom CO2 goes over 1000 ppm while the morning heating from R2 is on.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R4 opens the window and the radiator thermostat shuts off the heating that R2 started.
conflicts.explanation: The radiator thermostat's open-window detection depends on the window position, so R4's ventilation quietly cancels R2's heating.

conflicts.situation: Bedroom CO2 > 1000 ppm and outdoor PM2.5 > 35 at the same time.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The window is ordered both open and closed. It may flip back and forth, polluted air may come in, or CO2 may stay high.
conflicts.explanation: Both rules can fire at once and give opposite commands to window_bed.position.

conflicts.situation: At 07:00 while outdoor PM2.5 > 35.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R1 opens the window that R5 closed for pollution, so polluted air comes in while the purifier runs.
conflicts.explanation: The time-based open command ignores the air-quality closure and gives the opposite command to the same window.

conflicts.situation: At 07:30 while bedroom CO2 is still over 1000 ppm (window opened by R4).
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R3 closes the window during needed ventilation. CO2 rises again and R4 may reopen it, so the window can go back and forth.
conflicts.explanation: The scheduled close and the CO2-triggered open give opposite commands to window_bed.position, and both can apply at the same time.

conflicts.situation: Motion on the driveway triggers R1 and the halogen floodlight turns on.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The hot housing keeps the PIR reporting motion, so motion_drive never becomes false. R2 never fires and the floodlight stays on indefinitely, wasting energy and causing light pollution.
conflicts.explanation: R1's action (floodlight on) heats the PIR mounted under the housing, which keeps motion_drive true and stops R2's trigger from happening.

conflicts.situation: Home in night or away mode. Real motion turns the floodlight on through R1, and its heat keeps the PIR reporting motion.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: Continuous false motion keeps R3 firing, so the driveway camera records non-stop with false alarms, filling storage and hiding real events.
conflicts.explanation: The floodlight turned on by R1 keeps setting motion_drive true through heat, and that repeatedly triggers R3's recording even when no one is there.

conflicts.situation: After 23:00, R5 has switched off the outdoor lighting relay and someone moves on the driveway.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R1 sets the floodlight to on, but it has no power, so the driveway stays dark at night. This is a safety and security problem.
conflicts.explanation: The floodlight is wired to the outdoor lighting circuit that R5 cuts. Nothing in the rules shows this dependency.

conflicts.situation: At 23:00 R5 turns relay_outdoor off. No rule turns it back on, so at 19:00 the next day R4 tries to turn on the garden lights.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The garden lights' smart switch reports on, but the lights get no power and stay dark from then on.
conflicts.explanation: The garden lights depend on relay_outdoor, which R5 turns off and no rule restores, so R4 can't take effect.

conflicts.situation: Sunny but windy day: lux_balcony > 50000 while wind_speed > 40 km/h
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The awning is retracted and then extended again (or the other way round). If it ends up extended in strong wind, the manufacturer's safety limit is broken and the awning can be damaged.
conflicts.explanation: R1 sets awning.position to extended and R2 sets it to retracted, and both triggers can be true at the same time. Bright sun does not rule out strong wind.

conflicts.situation: Rainstorm: raining == true while wind_speed > 40 km/h
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R3 extends the awning in a storm, which goes against R2's safety retraction. The awning can be torn or damaged, or keep moving back and forth.
conflicts.explanation: Rain and strong wind often come together. R3 orders the awning extended and R2 orders it retracted at the same time.

conflicts.situation: Water is on the basement floor (moisture_basement == true) while home_power > 6000 W
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R3 cuts the basement circuit, so the sump pump that R1 turned on loses power and the basement floods.
conflicts.explanation: The sump pump is plugged into a socket on the basement circuit. Switching off relay_basement removes the pump's power no matter what R1 commanded.

conflicts.situation: At 02:00 the washer plug turns on while other loads are already high, so home_power goes above 6000 W
conflicts.undesired_outcome: Load shedding switches off the basement circuit, cutting power to the chest freezer (it can thaw) and to the sump pump (no flood protection).
conflicts.explanation: The washer's 2.5 kW heating element raises home_power, which fires R3. R3 then turns off relay_basement, which powers the freezer and sump pump.

conflicts.situation: After the 23:30 shutdown (R1), someone opens the balcony door, so R2 turns the AV receiver back on.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The receiver comes back on and, through HDMI-CEC, the TV wakes up too. This undoes R1's night shutdown of both the TV and the receiver.
conflicts.explanation: R2 only targets the receiver, but powering on the receiver wakes the TV through CEC, a link not stated in either rule. The result cancels R1's tv.power := off and av_receiver.power := off.

conflicts.situation: Motion is detected in the living room while it is darker than 30 lux, so R6 turns the floor lamp on. The lamp shines directly on the multisensor's light sensor.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The reading jumps above 200 lux, so R7 turns the lamp off right away. The room goes dark again, and the next motion turns the lamp back on. The lamp keeps flickering on and off and the occupant is left in the dark.
conflicts.explanation: The light from R6's action raises the sensor's lux_living reading, which triggers R7's turn-off rule. Since the reading is caused by the lamp itself, this is a false brightness reading, not a planned control loop.

conflicts.situation: At 19:00, R3 turns the floor lamp on. Its light hits the bookshelf multisensor and pushes lux_living above 200.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R7 turns the lamp off right away, so the scheduled evening light is cancelled.
conflicts.explanation: The lamp's own light raises the illuminance reading. R7 reads that as a bright room and turns off the lamp that R3 just turned on.

conflicts.situation: Daily at 06:30 when R1 turns on the steam shower generator; steam drifts from the bathroom onto the landing and the photoelectric smoke detector reports smoke_landing == true.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: False fire alarm: the indoor siren sounds and the house-wide air handler is shut off every morning without any real fire.
conflicts.explanation: R1's steam generator physically sets smoke_landing to true (photoelectric detector reads water droplets as smoke), which unexpectedly triggers R2's siren and HVAC shutdown.

conflicts.situation: After 22:00 (pump off until 08:00) while pool_temp < 26 C
conflicts.undesired_outcome: Pool heater is commanded on but its flow switch keeps the burner off, so the pool isn't heated overnight and the heating command silently fails
conflicts.explanation: R1 turns the circulation pump off; the heater's flow switch stops the burner without water flow, overriding R2's heating command.

conflicts.situation: Home is in away mode and pool_temp is or falls below 26 C
conflicts.undesired_outcome: Heater is turned off by R7 and switched back on by R2, so the gas heater runs while nobody is home
conflicts.explanation: R7 sets pool_heater.heating off on away mode while R2 sets it on whenever the water is below 26 C, with no away-mode check, so the rules give opposite commands to the same device.

conflicts.situation: Household leaves between 22:00 and 02:00: everyone_away becomes true (R1 sets mode=away) and living-room motion stops as people leave (R2 sets mode=night), firing nearly simultaneously.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: Hub mode ends up as 'night' (or flips away/night) while the flat is empty; via R7 the living room camera stops recording instead of recording (R6), and via R4 the thermostat is set to 19 C instead of 16 C (R3).
conflicts.explanation: R1 and R2 write incompatible values to hub.mode and both are triggered by the same departure event, since leaving also ends living-room motion; R2 does not check presence.

conflicts.situation: Every morning: R2 turns the bedroom radiator on at 06:45, then R1 opens the bedroom window at 07:00.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The TRV's window-open detection closes the radiator valve, so the morning heating stops after 15 minutes. The bedroom cools down, and heat is wasted while the window is open.
conflicts.explanation: Opening the window causes a temperature drop. The TRV detects this and turns heating off, which undoes R2's heating := on even though no rule says so.

conflicts.situation: Bedroom CO2 rises above 1000 ppm while the radiator is heating, for example during the morning heating period that starts at 06:45.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R4 opens the window, the TRV's window-open detection stops the radiator, and the planned heating is lost.
conflicts.explanation: R4's window opening affects trv_bed.heating physically and sets it to off, which cancels R2's heating := on.

conflicts.situation: Bedroom CO2 is above 1000 ppm and outdoor PM2.5 is above 35 at the same time.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R4 opens the window and R5 closes it. The window may go back and forth, or end up open and let polluted air in, or end up closed and leave CO2 high.
conflicts.explanation: Both rules can fire under the same conditions and set window_bed.position to opposite values.

conflicts.situation: At 07:00, outdoor PM2.5 is already above 35, and R5 closed the window earlier.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R1 reopens the window during high pollution. Polluted air comes in while the purifier is running.
conflicts.explanation: R1 opens the window at a fixed time and ignores R5's earlier close. Because R5 fires only when PM2.5 crosses 35, it does not close the window again.

conflicts.situation: CO2 goes above 1000 ppm shortly before 07:30, so R4 opens the window, and R3 closes it at 07:30 while CO2 is still high.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The window closes before the bedroom has been aired out. CO2 stays high, and R4 does not fire again because CO2 never drops back below the threshold.
conflicts.explanation: R3 closes the window at a fixed time and overrides R4's open command, which was meant to stay in effect until CO2 dropped.

conflicts.situation: Any time motion on the driveway triggers R1 and the halogen floodlight turns on.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The floodlight stays on indefinitely because R2 never fires. This wastes energy and causes light pollution.
conflicts.explanation: The PIR sensor sits under the hot halogen housing, so while the floodlight is on, motion_drive keeps reading true. R2's trigger (motion_drive == false) never happens.

conflicts.situation: The floodlight was turned on by R1, so the sensor is held at motion = true. The home is in night or away mode, or switches to it, and an intruder later enters the driveway.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The driveway camera does not start recording the real intrusion.
conflicts.explanation: The floodlight's heat holds the PIR at true. No new false-to-true motion event occurs, so R3 cannot fire on actual later motion.

conflicts.situation: After 23:00, when R5 has switched off the outdoor lighting circuit, and motion is detected on the driveway.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R1 fires, but the floodlight stays dark because it has no power. The driveway is unlit at night when it is most needed.
conflicts.explanation: The floodlight is wired to the outdoor lighting circuit controlled by relay_outdoor. Cutting the relay overrides R1's on command.

conflicts.situation: At 19:00 on any day after R5 has run at 23:00. No rule turns relay_outdoor back on.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R4 tries to turn on the garden lights, but they stay off because their circuit is unpowered.
conflicts.explanation: The garden lights are wired to the outdoor lighting circuit. R5 cuts it, and no rule restores it, so the smart switch command from R4 has no effect.

conflicts.situation: A bright, sunny day (lux_balcony > 50000) with strong wind (wind_speed > 40 km/h).
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The awning gets contradictory extend and retract commands. It may end up extended in wind above 40 km/h, which goes against the manufacturer's limit and risks damage.
conflicts.explanation: R1 extends the awning when it is bright and R2 retracts it when it is windy. Both triggers can be true at once, and nothing gives R2 priority.

conflicts.situation: A rainstorm where raining == true and wind_speed > 40 km/h, which often happen together.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The awning switches between extended and retracted. If R3 runs last, the awning stays extended in storm-force wind and can be torn or ripped off.
conflicts.explanation: R3 extends the awning when it rains and R2 retracts it when it is windy. Both conditions are common in the same storm and the rules give opposite commands to awning.position.

conflicts.situation: Home power use goes above 6000 W, so R3 switches off relay_basement. Then water reaches the basement floor (moisture_basement == true), or is already there.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R1 turns on the sump pump, but its socket has no power, so the basement floods. The chest freezer and dehumidifier also lose power.
conflicts.explanation: The sump pump is plugged into a socket on the basement circuit that relay_basement controls. Shedding load on that circuit cuts the pump's power, which R1 depends on, and no rule turns the circuit back on.

conflicts.situation: At 02:00, R4 turns on the heavy-duty washer plug while other loads are running, and the whole-home power goes above 6000 W.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The washer's load triggers R3, which switches off the basement circuit. The sump pump, freezer and dehumidifier lose power just to run the laundry, and they stay off after the washer stops at 04:00.
conflicts.explanation: R4's action raises home_power, the variable R3 triggers on. So a scheduled laundry run can cut power to safety-critical basement devices without anyone noticing.

conflicts.situation: Evening, motion detected in a dark living room (lux < 30); R6 turns on the floor lamp next to the bookshelf multisensor.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The lamp pushes the sensor reading above 200 lux, R7 turns the lamp off, so the occupant is left in the dark and the lamp may flicker on/off with each new motion event.
conflicts.explanation: The floor lamp stands beside the multisensor that measures lux_living, so R6's action directly raises the illuminance that triggers R7's off action.

conflicts.situation: At 19:00 R3 switches on the floor lamp located next to the lux sensor.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: Lux reading exceeds 200 from the lamp's own light, R7 turns the lamp off right after it was scheduled on.
conflicts.explanation: The lamp's light raises lux_living at the adjacent multisensor, triggering R7 and cancelling R3's intended effect.

conflicts.situation: Someone is on the balcony around 23:30 with the door open, or opens the balcony door after 23:30.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R1 cuts the balcony music while it is in use, or R2 turns the AV receiver back on after the scheduled shutdown (and via HDMI-CEC can also wake the TV), defeating the 23:30 off routine.
conflicts.explanation: R1 sets av_receiver.power off and R2 sets it on with independent triggers that can overlap in the late evening; CEC linkage additionally propagates the receiver power-on to the TV.

conflicts.situation: From 06:30 to 07:00 the steam shower generator is running and the bathroom door, which opens onto the landing, is open or opened, so steam reaches the landing.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: Steam sets off the photoelectric smoke detector on the landing when there is no fire. The siren sounds early in the morning and the air handler for the whole house shuts down.
conflicts.explanation: R1 fills the bathroom with steam. Photoelectric smoke detectors can mistake steam for smoke, so steam drifting onto the landing makes smoke_landing true and R2 fires even though there is no fire.

conflicts.situation: Between 22:00 and 08:00 the pump is off (R1) and the pool water drops below 26 C, so R2 turns the gas heater on.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The heater runs with no water flowing through it. Its flow switch stops it from firing or makes it short-cycle, so the pool is not heated, energy is wasted and the heater may wear out or fault.
conflicts.explanation: The gas heater has a built-in flow switch and only works while the circulation pump is running. R1 turns the pump off without checking whether R2 still wants heat.

conflicts.situation: The home is in away mode, so R7 has turned the heater off, and then the pool water drops below 26 C.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R2 turns the heater back on while the house is empty, which cancels the away-mode shutoff and wastes gas.
conflicts.explanation: R7 and R2 give opposite commands to pool_heater.heating, and R2 does not check home_mode, so both can apply at the same time.

conflicts.situation: Occupants leave between 22:00 and 02:00: everyone_away becomes true and living-room motion stops at the same time.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: Hub mode is set to both away (R1) and night (R2); the empty home can end up in night mode, so the away settings (16 C setpoint, camera recording) are overridden.
conflicts.explanation: R1 and R2 write different values to hub.mode and their triggers fire together when the last person leaves late in the evening. The outcome depends on which rule runs last.

conflicts.situation: Late-evening departure (22:00-02:00): the mode goes to away, then R2 switches it to night.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The living-room camera stops recording while the home is empty, defeating the security purpose of R6.
conflicts.explanation: R6 turns camera recording on in away mode and R7 turns it off in night mode. The away-to-night switch caused by R1 and R2 makes both fire in sequence, so the camera ends up off.

conflicts.situation: Bedroom CO2 is above 1000 ppm while outdoor PM2.5 is above 35.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The window flips between open and closed. Either polluted outdoor air comes in or CO2 stays at an unhealthy level.
conflicts.explanation: R4 opens window_bed because of high CO2 and R5 closes it because of high PM2.5. Both triggers can be active at the same time.

conflicts.situation: At 07:00, R5 has already closed the window because outdoor PM2.5 is above 35.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R1 opens the window while the outside air is polluted. Polluted air comes in and works against the purifier R5 turned on.
conflicts.explanation: R1 opens the window on a fixed schedule and does not check air quality. This overrides R5's protective close.

conflicts.situation: At 07:30, R4 has opened the window because bedroom CO2 is above 1000 ppm.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The window closes while CO2 is still high. Because R4 only fires when CO2 crosses 1000 ppm, it may not reopen the window, so the room stays poorly ventilated.
conflicts.explanation: R3 closes the window on a schedule and R4 needs it open. The two commands contradict each other.

conflicts.situation: Heating starts at 06:45 and the window opens at 07:00.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: Heat is wasted through the open window. The TRV's window-open detection notices the temperature drop and stops heating, so the morning heat-up fails.
conflicts.explanation: The open window affects the radiator through the room temperature and the TRV's window-open detection. Neither rule mentions this link.

conflicts.situation: Bedroom CO2 goes above 1000 ppm while the radiator is heating (for example, during the morning warm-up).
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The open window lets heat escape and sets off the TRV's window-open detection. Heating stops and the bedroom stays cold.
conflicts.explanation: Opening the window for CO2 indirectly turns off heating through the TRV's built-in window-open detection.

conflicts.situation: After 23:00, once R5 has opened the outdoor lighting relay, motion is detected on the driveway.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R1 sends the floodlight an 'on' command, but the floodlight has no power, so the driveway stays dark at night.
conflicts.explanation: relay_outdoor feeds the driveway floodlight. R5 cuts that circuit and nothing turns it back on, so R1's action does nothing.

conflicts.situation: At night or in away mode after 23:00, once R5 has switched off the outdoor lighting circuit, someone enters the driveway.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The driveway PIR sensor is mounted in the floodlight housing, so it likely loses power with the floodlight. It then can't report motion, and the camera never starts recording when it matters most.
conflicts.explanation: The PIR sensor probably depends on the floodlight's power supply, which runs through relay_outdoor. When R5 cuts the relay, the motion_drive trigger R3 relies on is disabled.

conflicts.situation: At 19:00 on the next evening after R5 opened the outdoor relay at 23:00, with no rule turning the relay back on.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R4 switches the garden lights' smart switch on, but the lights stay dark because their circuit has no power.
conflicts.explanation: The garden lights are on the outdoor lighting circuit that R5 switches off for good. No rule closes the relay again, so later 'on' commands to the garden lights fail.

conflicts.situation: Sunny, windy day: lux_balcony > 50000 and wind_speed > 40 km/h at the same time
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The awning is told to extend and retract. If R1 fires after R2, the awning stays extended in strong wind, against the manufacturer's limit, and can be damaged.
conflicts.explanation: R1 sets awning.position to extended and R2 sets it to retracted. Bright sun and strong wind often happen together, so both rules can be active at once.

conflicts.situation: Storm: raining == true and wind_speed > 40 km/h
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The awning is extended in storm wind to protect the furniture from rain, which goes against the manufacturer's rule to retract it above 40 km/h. The awning can be torn or damaged.
conflicts.explanation: R3 extends the awning when it rains and R2 retracts it when the wind is strong. Rain and strong wind often come together in storms, so the two rules give opposite commands to the same device.

conflicts.situation: Water is on the basement floor (moisture_basement == true) and R1 has turned on the sump pump, while total home power goes above 6000 W, for example during heavy appliance use or while the washer runs between 02:00 and 04:00.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R3 switches off the basement relay, which cuts power to the sump pump. The pump stops even though its switch is still on, so the basement can flood. The chest freezer and dehumidifier on the same circuit also lose power.
conflicts.explanation: The sump pump is plugged into a socket on the basement circuit that relay_basement controls. Neither rule states this dependency, so R3's load shedding quietly overrides R1's flood protection.

conflicts.situation: Balcony door opened shortly before 23:30 (receiver on for balcony music), then 23:30 arrives.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R1 switches the AV receiver off while someone is still out on the balcony listening to music.
conflicts.explanation: R2 sets av_receiver.power to on and R1 sets it to off. Both can be active at the same time, so the two rules fight over the receiver.

conflicts.situation: Balcony door opened after 23:30, once R1 has already turned the TV and receiver off.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The receiver turns back on and, through HDMI-CEC, probably wakes the TV too, undoing R1's night shut-off.
conflicts.explanation: The TV is linked to the receiver by HDMI with CEC enabled, so powering the receiver can power the TV. This dependency is not stated in either rule.

conflicts.situation: Motion in the living room while it is darker than 30 lux.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The lamp switches on, its own light pushes the reading above 200 lux, R7 turns it off, the room goes dark again and the lamp can keep switching on and off.
conflicts.explanation: The floor lamp stands next to the bookshelf multisensor, so turning the lamp on raises lux_living and triggers R7's turn-off rule.

conflicts.situation: At 19:00, when R3 turns the floor lamp on.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The scheduled evening light is turned off almost at once.
conflicts.explanation: The lamp's light hits the nearby multisensor and can push lux_living above 200, which triggers R7.

conflicts.situation: After 19:00, when motion in the living room stops or nobody is present.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The evening lamp set by the schedule is turned off by the no-motion rule, so the planned evening lighting gets cut off unexpectedly.
conflicts.explanation: R3 sets lamp_living to on unconditionally and R4 sets it to off, and both can apply in the same evening.

conflicts.situation: From 06:30 while the steam shower generator runs (until 07:00), especially when the bathroom door is opened onto the landing.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: Steam can falsely set off the photoelectric smoke detector on the landing. R2 then sounds the siren early in the morning and shuts off the air handler for all rooms.
conflicts.explanation: R1 turns on the steam generator, and steam escaping onto the landing can make the smoke detector report smoke. That makes R2 fire with no real fire.

conflicts.situation: Between 22:00 and 08:00 the pump is off (R1); pool_temp drops below 26 C and R2 turns the gas heater on.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The heater runs or is commanded on with no water circulation. Its flow switch blocks heating (the pool stays cold), or it risks overheating or damage.
conflicts.explanation: The gas heater's built-in flow switch depends on the circulation pump running. R1 cuts the pump at night, and R2 turns the heater on without checking the pump state.

conflicts.situation: home_mode is away (R7 turns the heater off) while pool_temp is or falls below 26 C.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R2 turns the heater back on, so it heats the pool while the house is empty and wastes gas.
conflicts.explanation: Both rules set pool_heater.heating to opposite values, and nothing in R2 excludes away mode, so they can both fire in the same situation.

conflicts.situation: Everyone leaves the flat between 22:00 and 02:00. R1 sets hub.mode to away, and because the living room is now empty, motion_living becomes false and R2 sets hub.mode to night.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The hub ends up in night mode instead of away while nobody is home. Away-mode behaviour (16 C setpoint, camera recording) is replaced by night-mode behaviour (19 C setpoint, camera off).
conflicts.explanation: R1 and R2 write different values to the same state, hub.mode. Their triggers can fire together because people leaving is exactly what makes living-room motion stop, and R2 does not check presence.

conflicts.situation: Late evening (22:00-02:00): the last person leaves, R1 switches to away and R6 starts recording. Motion then stops in the empty living room, so R2 switches to night and R7 fires.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The living room camera stops recording while the home is empty, which defeats the security purpose of away mode. Heating also goes back up to 19 C (R4), wasting energy.
conflicts.explanation: Leaving the home changes the motion context, which unexpectedly triggers R2's night mode. R7 then turns the camera off, undoing R6's away-mode recording.

conflicts.situation: The household is away (mode away from R1) and motion is detected in the living room between 06:00 and 10:00, for example from a pet, an intruder or a cleaner.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The mode switches to home while nobody is there. Away-mode protections no longer apply (camera recording is no longer tied to the mode) and the away heating setback is lost.
conflicts.explanation: R5 sets hub.mode to home based on motion alone, without checking everyone_away. This overrides the away mode that R1 set.

conflicts.situation: Bedroom CO2 > 1000 ppm while outdoor PM2.5 > 35
conflicts.undesired_outcome: Window is commanded open and closed at the same time; it may flip back and forth. Either polluted air comes in or CO2 builds up in the bedroom.
conflicts.explanation: R4 opens window_bed for ventilation while R5 closes it to keep out polluted air; both triggers can be true at once.

conflicts.situation: 07:00 while outdoor PM2.5 > 35
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The scheduled opening lets polluted outdoor air in while the purifier is running, which undoes R5's protection.
conflicts.explanation: R1 opens window_bed on schedule with no air-quality condition, contradicting R5's close command.

conflicts.situation: 07:30 while bedroom CO2 is still > 1000 ppm
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The window is closed while ventilation is still needed. CO2 builds up again and the window may repeatedly reopen and close.
conflicts.explanation: R3 closes window_bed on a fixed schedule regardless of CO2, opposing R4's open command.

conflicts.situation: Heating starts at 06:45, then the window opens at 07:00
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The thermostat's window-open detection stops heating, so the morning warm-up is cut off or the heat is wasted through the open window.
conflicts.explanation: The radiator thermostat with window-open detection turns heating off when the window opens, an unstated dependency between window_bed and trv_bed.

conflicts.situation: Morning heating is active (from 06:45) and bedroom CO2 goes above 1000 ppm, which is common after sleeping
conflicts.undesired_outcome: Opening the window triggers the thermostat's window-open detection, so heating is suspended or wasted during the morning heating period.
conflicts.explanation: R4's window opening is detected by the thermostat, which then overrides R2's heating-on command.

conflicts.situation: After 23:00, when motion is detected on the driveway
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The floodlight doesn't turn on despite the motion, so the driveway stays dark
conflicts.explanation: R5 cuts power to the outdoor lighting circuit, which feeds the driveway floodlight. R1's 'on' command has no effect, and no rule restores the relay.

conflicts.situation: After 23:00 in night or away mode, when someone enters the driveway
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The camera doesn't record intruders, because motion is never detected
conflicts.explanation: The driveway motion sensor is mounted under the floodlight housing and is likely powered from the outdoor lighting circuit. When R5 switches that circuit off, the sensor goes dead and R3 can never fire, even though the camera itself is powered over Ethernet from the house.

conflicts.situation: At 19:00 on any day after R5 has run at 23:00
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The garden lights stay off in the evening
conflicts.explanation: R5 leaves the outdoor lighting relay off and no rule turns it back on. R4's command to the garden lights' own switch has no effect because the circuit has no power.

conflicts.situation: Sunny, windy day: lux_balcony > 50000 while wind_speed > 40 km/h
conflicts.undesired_outcome: Awning gets extended and retracted over and over. If it ends up extended, it stays out in wind above the manufacturer's 40 km/h limit and can be damaged.
conflicts.explanation: R1 extends the awning on bright sun and R2 retracts it on strong wind. Neither rule checks the other's sensor, so both can fire at the same time with opposite commands.

conflicts.situation: Storm: raining == true and wind_speed > 40 km/h
conflicts.undesired_outcome: Awning is extended during a storm, against the manufacturer's wind limit. This risks tearing the fabric or the mechanism, and the awning keeps switching between extended and retracted.
conflicts.explanation: Rain and strong wind often happen together. R3 extends the awning for rain while R2 retracts it for wind, giving opposite commands to the same device.

conflicts.situation: Whole-home consumption exceeds 6000 W (e.g. heavy appliances running) while water is present on the basement floor (moisture_basement == true).
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R3 cuts the basement circuit, de-energising the sump pump; R1's 'sump pump on' command has no effect and the basement floods (freezer and dehumidifier also lose power).
conflicts.explanation: The sump pump is plugged into a socket on the basement circuit controlled by relay_basement. Load shedding by R3 removes its power supply, which R1 implicitly depends on.

conflicts.situation: Balcony door is open / opened around or after 23:30 (R2 turns the receiver on, R1 turns it off at 23:30)
conflicts.undesired_outcome: Balcony music is cut off at 23:30 while someone is on the balcony, or the receiver is turned back on after the night shutdown; the receiver state flips between on and off
conflicts.explanation: R1 sets av_receiver.power off and R2 sets it on; both can apply in the same late-evening period, so they give opposite commands to the same device.

conflicts.situation: After 23:30 the TV and receiver have been switched off by R1, then the balcony door is opened
conflicts.undesired_outcome: Turning the receiver on to play balcony music also wakes the TV through HDMI-CEC, undoing R1's TV shutdown (and CEC power-off at 23:30 can also cut the receiver while music is playing)
conflicts.explanation: The TV and receiver are linked by HDMI with CEC enabled, which is not stated in either rule, so powering the receiver on can power the TV on too.

conflicts.situation: At 19:00 R3 turns on the floor lamp, which stands right next to the bookshelf multisensor
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The lamp likely pushes lux_living above 200, so R7 immediately turns it off and the scheduled evening light does not stay on
conflicts.explanation: R3's action raises the illuminance reading that triggers R7, which reverses R3's action.

conflicts.situation: Living room is dark (<30 lux) and motion is detected; the lamp is next to the light sensor
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The lamp switches on, raises the sensor reading above 200 lux, R7 switches it off, the room is dark again and the next motion turns it back on, so the lamp keeps flickering on and off
conflicts.explanation: The lamp's own light is measured by the sensor that both rules depend on, so R6's action fires R7 and R7's action re-enables R6.

conflicts.situation: Between 06:30 and 07:00, R1 has the steam shower generator running. Steam escapes through the bathroom door, which opens onto the landing, and reaches the photoelectric smoke detector there.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The smoke detector reads steam as smoke and sets smoke_landing to true. R2 then sounds the indoor siren early in the morning and shuts off the air handler for the whole home, even though there is no fire.
conflicts.explanation: Photoelectric smoke detectors are known to false-alarm on dense steam or water vapour. The device description says the steam bathroom opens onto the landing, so R1's action can trigger R2 when it shouldn't.

conflicts.situation: Between 22:00 and 08:00, after R1 has turned off the circulation pump, the pool water drops below 26 C and R2 turns the pool heater on.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The heater is commanded on but cannot heat because no water is flowing. The pool keeps cooling overnight, and the gas heater may cycle or report faults while the system assumes it is heating.
conflicts.explanation: The gas heater has a built-in flow switch, so it only fires when the pump is circulating water. R1 cuts the pump at night, which silently stops R2's heating action from working.

conflicts.situation: The home is in away mode and the pool temperature is below 26 C, for example when R2 fires after R7 has already turned the heater off.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R7 turns the heater off to save energy while nobody is home, but R2 turns it back on as soon as the water is colder than 26 C. The heater runs while everyone is away, or flips between on and off.
conflicts.explanation: Both rules set pool_heater.heating to opposite values. R2 has no condition that stops it in away mode, so their triggers can overlap.

conflicts.situation: Household leaves between 22:00 and 02:00: everyone_away becomes true (R1 sets mode=away) and living-room motion stops as people leave (R2 sets mode=night), firing nearly simultaneously.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: Hub mode ends up as 'night' (or flips away/night) while the flat is empty; via R7 the living room camera stops recording instead of recording (R6), and via R4 the thermostat is set to 19 C instead of 16 C (R3).
conflicts.explanation: R1 and R2 write incompatible values to hub.mode and both are triggered by the same departure event, since leaving also ends living-room motion; R2 does not check presence.

conflicts.situation: Bedroom CO2 is above 1000 ppm while outdoor PM2.5 is above 35.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R4 opens the bedroom window and R5 closes it. The window can keep opening and closing, either polluted air comes in or CO2 keeps building up, and the purifier runs while the window is open.
conflicts.explanation: Both rules set window_bed.position to opposite values. Once R5 closes the window, CO2 keeps rising, so R4 opens it again.

conflicts.situation: At 07:00, when outdoor PM2.5 is above 35 (R5 has already closed the window or fires around the same time).
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R1 opens the window on its schedule even though the air outside is polluted. This undoes R5's protective close and lets in fine particles while the purifier is running.
conflicts.explanation: R1 opens the window on a schedule without checking air quality, which overrides R5's command to close it.

conflicts.situation: At 07:30, while bedroom CO2 is still above 1000 ppm and R4 has opened the window.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R3 closes the window while the room still needs fresh air, so CO2 rises further. Because R4 only fires when CO2 crosses the threshold, it may not reopen the window, and the room stays stuffy.
conflicts.explanation: R3 closes the window on a schedule without checking CO2, which overrides R4's ventilation command.

conflicts.situation: R2 starts the radiator at 06:45 to warm the bedroom, then R1 opens the window at 07:00.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The TRV's window-open detection notices the sudden temperature drop and stops heating, so the morning warm-up fails. Until it stops, heat also goes out the open window.
conflicts.explanation: Opening the window physically cools the room. The TRV's window-open detection then cancels the heating that R2 started, and neither rule mentions this dependency.

conflicts.situation: After 23:00, when R5 has switched relay_outdoor off and motion is detected on the driveway (motion_drive == true).
conflicts.undesired_outcome: R1 commands the floodlight on, but it has no power, so the driveway stays dark at night.
conflicts.explanation: relay_outdoor feeds the outdoor lighting circuit, which includes the driveway floodlight. Cutting the relay silently overrides R1's action.

conflicts.situation: After 23:00, with home_mode night or away and the outdoor circuit switched off by R5, someone enters the driveway.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The driveway motion sensor, mounted in the floodlight housing, probably loses power along with the floodlight, so no motion event occurs and the camera does not record intruders.
conflicts.explanation: The sensor appears to share the floodlight's circuit (likely, not confirmed in the data). Without power it cannot set motion_drive, so R3 is never triggered even though the PoE camera itself still has power.

conflicts.situation: At 19:00 on any day after R5 has switched off relay_outdoor at 23:00; no rule ever switches the relay back on.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The garden lights get R4's 'on' command but stay dark because their supply circuit is still off.
conflicts.explanation: The garden lights are on the outdoor lighting circuit controlled by relay_outdoor. R5 cuts that circuit permanently, so R4's action has no effect.

conflicts.situation: A bright, windy day: lux_balcony > 50000 while wind_speed > 40 km/h.
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The awning switches between extended and retracted, and may end up extended in strong wind. The manufacturer forbids this, so the awning could be damaged.
conflicts.explanation: R1 extends the awning because of sun and R2 retracts it because of wind. Both conditions can be true at the same time, so the two rules send opposite commands to the awning.

conflicts.situation: A storm with rain and wind above 40 km/h (raining == true and wind_speed > 40).
conflicts.undesired_outcome: The awning may be extended in storm-force wind, which the manufacturer forbids, and could be torn or damaged.
conflicts.explanation: R3 extends the awning when it rains and R2 retracts it when the wind is strong. Rain and strong wind often come together, so the two rules send opposite commands to the awning.

conflicts.explanation: Both rules set av_receiver.power to opposite values, and nothing in either rule limits them to different times or states.

conflicts.situation: After 19:00, when R3 has turned the floor lamp on and living-room motion then stops (for example, someone sits still or leaves briefly).
